sentences.text: You probably know the Persians as the villains.
A faceless army of slaves, driven forward with whips against 300 free men in a narrow pass.
That picture comes from the other side.
Almost everything we were taught about Persia was written by Greeks.
The people Persia was at war with.
Here is what the Greeks tended to leave out.
The men who built the Persian capital were paid, and we still have the receipts.
Greeks fought on the Persian side too.
The Athenian who beat the Persian fleet at Salamis later moved to Persia and took a job from the king.
And the man who finally conquered the empire ended up dressed as a Persian king, running the place almost exactly as he found it.
Persia was the largest state the world had yet seen, from the Balkans to the Indus, dozens of peoples, dozens of languages about 3000 miles from end to end.
It lasted some 220 years.
That is less time than the United States has existed.
So how do you run an empire 3000 miles wide on horseback?
Let's find out.
It takes 20 minutes.

Around 550 BC, the Middle East is a neighbourhood of old, rich kingdoms, Babylon with its towers and its bankers, Lydia, where coins were invented, Egypt, already ancient, and the Medes, horse lords of the Iranian Plateau.
The Persians are nobody yet.
They are herders and horsemen in a dry southern corner of today's Iran, a land called Passe, and they answer to the Medes.
Herodotus says Persian boys were taught three things only, to ride, to shoot a bow, and to tell the truth.
Then one of their kings, Cyrus, starts winning.
First he takes over the Medes, and part of the Median Army simply changes sides.
Next he marches across the whole of Anatolia and takes Lydia, the kingdom of Cressus, whose name still means rich.
Then the Greek cities on the coast of what is now Turkey, then east into Central Asia.
The Lydian War comes with a story.
Before attacking, Cressus asks the oracle at Delphi whether he should fight the Persians.
The answer?
If he sends an army against them, he will destroy a great empire.
He takes that as a yes.
The empire he destroys is his own.
Herodotus says Cyrus spared him and kept him as an advisor.
In about 20 years, a people from the edge of the map owns most of it.
One great prize is left.
Babylon is the biggest city on Earth, behind walls so thick Herodotus claims that a chariot can turn around on top.
In 539 BC, Cyrus beats its army in the field and the city opens its gates to him without a siege.
And here he does something unusual.
The empires before him, Assyria and Babylon, ruled by terror.
Beat a people, deport them, smash their temples.
Cyrus does the opposite.
And he puts it in writing.
On a clay cylinder, small enough to hold in two hands, in the Babylonian's own language, he announces that their god, Marduk, personally chose him.
He repairs temples, he sends captured statues of gods back to their cities and deported peoples back to their homes.
Among those who go home are the Jews, exiles in Babylon for half a century.
The cylinder never mentions them, but the Bible does.
It calls Cyrus a foreign king the Lord's anointed.
Today a replica of that cylinder sits at the United Nations and it is often called the first charter of human rights.
It isn't.
Nobody in the 6th century BC had heard of human rights and the curators who look after the real cylinder at the British Museum say so plainly.
It is royal PR.
But it is PR with a new idea inside.
Cyrus has worked out that it is cheaper to be welcomed than to be feared.
Keep your gods, keep your priests, keep your laws.
Just send the taxes to me.
Cyrus dies, Herodotus says, fighting nomads in Central Asia.
His son, Cambyses, adds Egypt, the last of the old great powers, and then dies on the way home, and the whole thing nearly falls apart.
What happens next, we know mainly from one man, and he is not neutral.
According to Darius, a priest had stolen the throne by pretending to be Cyrus' other son.
Darius, a distant relative who carried the king's spear, kills the imposter with six friends and takes the crown.
Some historians suspect a simpler story.
The imposter was the real prince, and Darius was the usurper.
Either way, the empire explodes.
Babylon, media, elam, Egypt, provinces rebel one after another.
Darius says he fought 19 battles in a single year and captured nine kings.
Then he does what any modern politician would do.
He takes control of the narrative.
On a cliff at Behistun, 100 metres above the main road, he carves his version in three languages, with himself standing on the imposter's chest.
Copies go out across the empire.
One has turned up in Egypt on papyrus in a fourth language.
His enemies, the text says, followed the lie.
He serves the truth.
Think of it as a press release carved in stone.
It had a second life, too.
In the 1830s and 40s, a British officer, Henry Rawlinson, copied it off the cliff face, and those three parallel texts became the key to reading cuneiform.
Cyrus built the empire.
Darius turns it into a machine.
He cuts the map into provinces, each run by a governor called a satrap.
We still use that word for a boss who behaves like a small king.
Herodotus counts 20 of them.
Each owes a fixed amount of silver a year.
No more send what you can.
A number written down.
Persians grumbled that Cyrus had been a father and Darius was a shopkeeper.
To keep the satraps honest, Greek writers say, Fortress commanders answered straight to the king, and royal inspectors turned up without warning.
The Greeks called them the king's eyes.
Darius mints a gold coin with a royal archer on it, and it becomes the hard currency of its age.
For paperwork across the provinces, the empire uses Aramaic, which is not Persian at all.
It is simply the language most clerks already know.
Even at the capital, the accounts are kept in Elomite, the language of the people who were there first.
Persian is for monuments.
And nobody is asked to become Persian.
Egypt keeps its pharaoh.
It just happens to be Darius carved in Egyptian dress.
Babylon keeps its temples, Judea its law, the Greek cities their own local rulers.
An empire this size has one enemy more dangerous than any rebel.
Distance.
From the capital at Sousa to the western end at Sardis is about 2700 kilometers.
On foot, that is three months.
So Persia organizes the road.
Much of it is older than the Persians.
They inherit it the way they inherit everything useful.
What they add is a system, more than 100 stations with fresh horses and fresh riders waiting.
A message is passed on like a baton in Aurelée and it crosses the empire in about nine days.
Herodotus, who was not easily impressed by Persians, wrote that nothing mortal travels faster and that neither snow nor rain nor heat nor darkness stops these couriers.
If that sounds familiar, a version of it is carved across the front of the old main post office in New York.
And in Egypt, Darius links the Nile to the Red Sea with a canal.
His inscription there boils down to this.
I ordered this canal dug.
It was dug.
Ships went from Egypt to Persia as I wished.
An ancestor of the Sousa canal more than 2000 years early.
To show what all this is for, Darius builds a new ceremonial capital in the Persian homeland.
The Greeks will call it Persepolis.
Walk up its great staircase and look at the walls.
Assyrian palaces were decorated with sieges, impaled prisoners and piles of heads.
Here, there is not one battle scene.
Instead, 23 delegations, carved in stone, climbed the stairs with gifts.
Lydians with fine vessels, Arabs leading a camel, Africans carrying an elephant tusk.
An usher takes each leader by the hand.
The message is not, we crushed you.
It is, everyone has a place, and here it is.
At Sussa, Darius lists who built his palace.
Cedar from Lebanon.
Gold from Sardis and Bactria.
Ivory from Africa and India.
Greek stone cutters, Egyptian goldsmiths, Babylonian brickmakers.
The palace is a map of the empire.
And we can check him.
In 1933, archaeologists found an office archive inside the fortification wall of Persepolis.
Some 20 ,000 clay tablets and fragments.
The remains of around 15 ,000 documents covering just 16 years.
They are receipts.
Bali for a gang of foreign workers.
Wine for a traveler on his way from India.
Feed for horses.
Offerings for the gods and not only the Persian ones.
These workers were not free in our sense.
Many were probably deported there.
But they were counted, fed and paid down to the last jug.
The most powerful man on earth ran his capital like an accountant.
The Greeks remembered the whips.
The tablets show the spreadsheets.
None of this makes Persia gentle.
It is an empire.
It takes your silver and your sons.
When Darius catches a rebel king, he tells us himself what he did.
Cut off the man's nose, ears and tongue.
Put out one eye, chained him at the palace gate for everyone to see, and then impaled him.
Tolerance is the offer.
That is what refusing it looks like.
In 499 BC, the Greek cities of the Turkish coast refuse.
The revolt starts in Miletus, whose leader, Aristagoras, announces that the city is now a democracy.
Athens sends 20 ships and the rebels burn Sardis, the Persian provincial capital.
It takes Persia six years to crush them.
In 494 BC, at the naval battle of Laid, the Greek fleet falls apart when the Samians sail away, Herodotus says.
Miletus, the greatest of the rebel cities, is taken.
Its men are killed, its women and children enslaved, and the survivors are marched to the shore of the Persian Gulf at the far end of the empire.
And then, in 492 BC, the Persian general, Mardonius, does something no one expects.
He removes the tyrants who had ruled those Greek cities for Persia and sets up democracies instead.
The great king's general, installing democracy because it happens to keep the cities quiet.
Persia has no ideology except what works.
But Darius has not forgotten Athens.
Herodotus says he ordered a servant to remind him of it three times a day.
In 490 BC, a Persian force lands at Marathon, a day's march from Athens, and loses.
For Athenians, this becomes a founding legend.
For Persia, it is a failed expedition on a distant frontier, and Darius has bigger problems.
Egypt revolts.
Then, he dies.
His son Xerxes decides to settle the matter properly.
The preparations take years, and they are an engineering show.
Across the hellespont, more than a kilometer of open water, he lays two bridges of boats.
The first pair is wrecked by a storm, and Herodotus says Xerxes had the sea -wipped and fetters thrown into it.
The second pair holds.
And through the neck of the Athos Peninsula, where a storm had wrecked an earlier fleet, he digs a ship canal two kilometers long.
Later writers called that a Greek tall tail.
In the 1990s, geophysicists found the canal, buried exactly where Herodotus put it.
How big was the army?
Herodotus counts 1 ,700 ,000 foot soldiers alone, drinking rivers dry.
Modern historians guess at a tenth of that or less, which is still enormous.
At its core are the Persians themselves, and above all, 10 ,000 men Herodotus calls the Immortals.
The name, he says, comes from the fact that the unit is always exactly 10 ,000.
When a man dies or falls sick, a replacement steps in at once, so the cause never seems to lose anyone.
Around them marches a crowd of other peoples, each in its own dress and with its own weapons.
Herodotus lists dozens of them.
At Thermopylae, it meets the 300 Spartans, plus several thousand other Greeks who usually get cut from the film.
The Immortals fight there too.
They hold the past for three days, until a local man shows the Persians a mountain path.
And Xerxes is not short of Greek help.
An exiled king of Sparta rides with him as an advisor.
Thessaly, Macedon and soon Thebes are in his camp.
One of his naval commanders is a queen from a Greek city, Artemisia.
A large part of the Greek world is on the Persians side.
Xerxes takes Athens and burns the temples on the Acropolis.
For a moment, the war looks one.
Then comes the trap.
The Athenian commander Themistocles sends a servant to Xerxes with a false message.
The Greeks are quarrelling and will slip away tonight, so block the strait.
Xerxes believes it and sends his fleet into the narrow channel of Salamis, where numbers are useless.
The Greeks wreck it.
One person comes out of it well.
Artemesia, the queen of Halekanassus, who had warned Xerxes not to fight there.
Herodotus says that when a Greek ship chases her, she rams a ship from her own side, so the pursuer takes her for a friend and turns away.
Xerxes, watching from the shore, thinks she has sunk a Greek ship.
My men, he says, have become women, and my women men!
Xerxes goes home.
The army he leaves behind is beaten the next year at Plataea.
For the Greeks, this is the moment that defines them.
They will write about it for centuries, and that is why you have heard of it.
Now look at the same events from Sousa.
The Empire has lost a campaign at its far western edge, and over time, a strip of coastline.
It has not lost a single province that matters.
Persia will go on for another 150 years.
No Persian account of the war survives at all.
And Persia learns!
If you can't beat the Greeks, rent them.
Themistocles, the Athenian who planned the victory at Salamis, is later driven out by his own city.
He flees to the Persian court, learns Persian, and ends his days as a governor for the great king.
When Athens and Sparta tear each other apart in the Peloponnesian War, Persian gold pays for the Spartan fleet.
A Persian prince governing Asia Minor, Cyrus the Younger, hands the Spartan Admiral Lysander his entire treasury, and the crews get a pay rise.
In 405 BC at Aegos Potamie, Lysander catches the Athenian fleet on the beach and captures most of it.
Athens surrenders the next year.
When 10 ,000 Greek soldiers need work, they march into Asia as hired spears in a Persian civil war.
The same prince wants his brothers thrown.
He is killed at Kunaxa in 401 BC, and the Greeks have to fight their way home through hostile country.
One of them, Xenophon, wrote the book.
And in 387 BC, the Greek cities, exhausted by yet another war among themselves, accept a peace treaty.
Its terms are sent down from Sousa, and it is known by the Persian rulers' title, the King's Peace.
Its first clause says the Greek cities of Asia belong to him.
What Xerxes lost with an army, his great -grandson wins back with a purse, and the Greeks sign for it.
The Greeks also tell a story to explain all this.
Persia is rotting.
Soft kings, scheming queens, too much luxury.
It is a good story, and historians repeated it for 2 ,000 years.
The evidence says otherwise.
Around 340 BC, Persia reconquers Egypt, which had broken away for 60 years.
The treasury is full.
The roads work.
What Persia does not have is an answer to the new army built in Macedon.
In 334 BC, Alexander leads it into Asia.
Three great battles in three years, and the King of Kings, Darius III, is running east, where one of his own satraps murders him.
Alexander reaches Persepolis and burns the palace.
After a long night of drinking, most ancient writers say, revenge for the Acropolis, 150 years late.
But watch what he does next.
He gives Darius a royal funeral and hunts down the killer, a satrap who has already declared himself king.
He keeps the provinces, the taxes, the roads, and a good number of the Persian governors.
He starts wearing Persian royal dress.
He asks his Macedonians to bow to him the Persian way, and they are appalled.
At Sousa, he marries a daughter of Darius and has about 80 of his officers marry Persian noblewomen in the same ceremony.
The French historian Pierre Breon argues that in many ways, Alexander acted as the last of the Aquiminids.
He did not destroy the Persian Empire, he took it over.
When he died seven years later, his generals carved it up and kept the machinery.
Provinces, royal roads, a state courier service.
You will meet them again in almost every empire that followed, Rome included.
The Persians left words behind as well.
Their walled royal parks were called something like Paridazar.
The Greeks heard Paridazos.
We say paradise.
Even the name is a souvenir.
Persia is what the Greeks called the whole country, after one province, Parsa.
The people who live there use a different and very old name, and in 1935 they asked the rest of the world to use it too.
Iran.
But the best answer to our question is one of those clay tablets from Persepolis.
Some of them small enough to hide in your fist.
It records that women on a work team have given birth, and are issued extra rations of wine or beer and grain, twice as much if the baby is a boy.
Nobody said this was a fair world.
Think about what that means.
25 centuries ago, in a state stretching across three continents, a clerk knew that a woman in a work gang had just had a child, and that the king owed her an extra ration.
That is how you rule an empire 3000 miles wide on horseback, not by making everyone the same, by letting them stay different, and writing everything down.
The Greeks won the story.
The Persians built the system.
Every empire since has borrowed from both.
That was Persia.
If you enjoyed these 20 minutes, subscribe, and tell us in the comments which civilization you want to see next.
